paragraphs.heading: A spinning column of air
paragraphs.text: A tornado, or twister, is a column of air spinning fast and violently, stretching from the ground up to the base of a cumulonimbus or cumulus cloud. To count as a tornado, the spinning column must touch both the ground and the cloud. The word means the whirling wind itself, not the cloud that may form around it.

paragraphs.heading: Size and power
paragraphs.text: Most tornadoes have winds under 180 km/h (110 mph), are about 80 m (250 ft) wide, and travel a few kilometres before they fade. The most extreme ones are another matter. Their winds can top 480 km/h (300 mph), they can be over 3 km (2 mi) wide, and they can keep touching the ground over a track longer than 100 km (62 mi).

paragraphs.heading: Seen and unseen
paragraphs.text: A tornado is not always visible. Its fast winds and rapid spin create very low pressure, and that usually makes water vapour in the air condense into droplets, forming a funnel cloud. Near the ground there is often a swirling cloud of dust and debris. Rain or dust can hide a tornado entirely, which makes it especially dangerous, since even experienced meteorologists may not see it. From far away it is also hard to tell a funnel cloud from a tornado, because most tornadoes already blow hard at the surface while the funnel is still above the ground.

paragraphs.heading: Where they happen
paragraphs.text: The United States has far more tornadoes than any other country, especially in central and southeastern areas known as Tornado Alley. They also strike in South Africa, much of Europe, western and eastern Australia, New Zealand, Bangladesh and eastern India, Japan, the Philippines, and Uruguay and Argentina.

paragraphs.heading: Rating by damage
paragraphs.text: Tornadoes are rated by the damage they leave behind. The Fujita scale, now replaced in some countries by the Enhanced Fujita scale, runs from F0 or EF0, which harms trees but not solid buildings, to F5 or EF5, which tears buildings off their foundations and can bend large skyscrapers. The TORRO scale works in a similar way, from T0, for the very weakest tornadoes, up to T11, for the most powerful known. Experts may also study Doppler radar data, photogrammetry and swirl marks on the ground to settle a rating.

paragraphs.heading: Spotting them and their families
paragraphs.text: Tornadoes can be picked up before or as they form with pulse-Doppler radar, which shows tell-tale patterns such as hook echoes or debris balls, and the work of storm spotters helps detect them as well. A single storm sometimes makes more than one tornado, at the same time or one after another, and such a group is called a tornado family. When a large storm system spawns several tornadoes with no break in activity, it counts as a tornado outbreak.

paragraphs.heading: Where the word comes from
paragraphs.text: The word comes from the Spanish tronada, meaning 'thunderstorm'. Its English spelling was nudged by another Spanish word, tornado, from tornar, 'to twist, turn'. Its cousin in name is the derecho, Spanish for 'straight', a widespread windstorm that blows in a straight line rather than packing into a small area.
